dryRun.title: Find the number that appears once in [4, 1, 2, 1, 2] by XOR-ing everything
dryRun.note: XOR has two rules: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x, and the order does not matter. So every pair cancels out, and only the number that has no partner stays: 4.

think.q: console.log(5 ^ 5, 5 ^ 0, 6 ^ 3)
why: A number XOR itself is 0, and XOR with 0 changes nothing. 6 is 110 and 3 is 011, so 6 ^ 3 = 101 = 5.
XOR answers the question "which bits are different?".

think.q:
let r = 0
for (const x of [4, 1, 2, 1, 2]) r ^= x
console.log(r)
why: The two 1s cancel, the two 2s cancel, and 4 is left. The answer needs O(n) time and O(1) space, with no hash map.
It works for any order of the input.
think.exec:
let r = 0
for (const x of [4, 1, 2, 1, 2]) r ^= x
console.log(r)

think.q:
let a = 3, b = 5
a ^= b
b ^= a
a ^= b
console.log(a, b)
why: After the three steps the values are swapped: 5 and 3. Each step uses the cancel rule: a ^ b ^ b = a.
It is a nice trick, but in real code [a, b] = [b, a] is clearer.
think.exec:
let a = 3, b = 5
a ^= b
b ^= a
a ^= b
console.log(a, b)

think.q:
const nums = [3, 0, 1]
let x = nums.length
for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) x ^= i ^ nums[i]
console.log(x)

The array should hold every number from 0 to 3 once, but one is missing.
why: XOR all the indexes (and the length) and all the values together. Everything that is present appears twice and cancels out, so the missing number is left: 2.
This avoids the overflow risk of summing very large numbers.
think.exec:
const nums = [3, 0, 1]
let x = nums.length
for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) x ^= i ^ nums[i]
console.log(x)

think.q: Which properties make the XOR trick work?
opts: x ^ x = 0, x ^ 0 = x, and the order of XOR-ing does not matter
XOR always returns the bigger number
XOR only works on positive numbers
why: Because the order does not matter you can imagine the pairs standing next to each other, and each pair becomes 0.
It also works for negative numbers, because JavaScript XOR treats them as 32-bit integers.

try.task: Write singleNumber(nums). Every number appears twice except one, which appears once. Return that number. Use O(1) extra space.
try.hint: Start with result = 0 and XOR every number into it.

checks.verify: const a = []; for (let i = 1; i <= 100000; i++) a.push(i, i); a.push(424242); const t0 = Date.now(); assert(singleNumber(a) === 424242 && Date.now() - t0 < 100, "wrong or too slow")

takeaway.key: XOR cancels equal pairs: x ^ x = 0, x ^ 0 = x, in any order. So "everything appears twice except one" is a single loop with O(1) space.
mistakes: Using a hash map when O(1) space is asked.
Using + or - instead of ^.
Forgetting that it only works if the other numbers come in pairs.
Expecting it to work on numbers larger than 32 bits.

dryRun.title: Bit operations on 10 (binary 1010)
rows: 0, so the bit is not set
dryRun.note: Four moves cover almost everything: mask 1 << i, test with &, set with |, clear with & ~, toggle with ^.

think.q: console.log(1 << 4, 20 >> 2, -8 >> 1, -8 >>> 28)
why: << 4 multiplies by 16, and >> 2 divides 20 by 4. The sign-keeping shift -8 >> 1 is -4. The unsigned shift -8 >>> 28 treats -8 as 0xFFFFFFF8, so the top 4 bits (all ones) remain: 15.
>> keeps the sign; >>> fills with zeros.

think.q: console.log((10 >> 0) & 1, (10 >> 1) & 1)
why: 10 is 1010. Bit 0 (the rightmost) is 0 and bit 1 is 1. Shifting right by i puts bit i at position 0, and & 1 keeps only that bit.
This is the standard way to read bit i.

think.q: console.log(1 << 2 + 1, (1 << 2) + 1)
why: Addition binds tighter than a shift, so 1 << 2 + 1 means 1 << 3, which is 8. With brackets we get 4 + 1 = 5.
The same trap exists for & and ==. Use brackets around bit operations.

think.q: console.log(1 << 31, 1 << 32)
why: JavaScript bit operations work on 32-bit signed integers. Bit 31 is the sign bit, so 1 << 31 is negative. The shift count wraps modulo 32, so 1 << 32 is 1 << 0 = 1.
For bigger numbers use BigInt or plain arithmetic.

think.q: To count the 1-bits of a non-negative number n you loop with n & 1 and then shift n. Which shift avoids an endless loop when n has its top bit set?
why: With >> a negative number keeps its sign bit, so it never reaches 0. The unsigned shift >>> fills with zeros, so the loop ends after at most 32 steps.
The brackets-and-shifts details are the reason this lesson is worth a look.

try.task: Write countBits(n). n is an integer from 0 to 4294967295 (32 bits, treated as unsigned). Return how many bits are 1. Use shifts and masks.
try.hint: Loop 32 times: add n & 1 to a counter and do n = n >>> 1. Use >>>, not >>.

takeaway.key: Bits: mask 1 << i, test &, set |, clear & ~, toggle ^. JavaScript uses 32-bit signed integers: use >>> for unsigned shifts and brackets for precedence.
mistakes: Writing a & 1 == 1 (precedence).
Using >> on numbers with the top bit set.
Shifting by 32 or more.
Using bit operations on numbers larger than 32 bits.

dryRun.title: n & (n - 1) removes the lowest set bit. Starting with 12
rows: the lowest 1 bit is gone: 1 bit removed
a power of two has only one bit, so one step gives 0
dryRun.note: Subtracting 1 flips the lowest 1 bit to 0 and every 0 below it to 1. AND-ing with the original clears exactly that lowest 1 bit. The loop while (n) n &= n - 1 runs once per set bit.

think.q: console.log(12 & 11, 8 & 7, 10 & 9)
why: Each time exactly one 1 bit, the lowest, disappears.

think.q:
let n = 13, c = 0
while (n) {
  n &= n - 1
  c++
}
console.log(c)
why: 13 is 1101, which has three 1 bits, so the loop runs three times: 1101 → 1100 → 1000 → 0000.
It is faster than checking every bit when only a few bits are set.

think.q: console.log([1, 6, 16, 0].map((n) => n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) === 0).join())
why: A power of two has exactly one 1 bit, so removing it leaves 0. 6 (110) has two bits. 0 has none, so the n > 0 check is needed.
This one-liner is a classic interview question.

think.q: console.log(12 & -12)
why: In two's complement, -n flips all bits above the lowest 1 and keeps the lowest 1. The AND leaves only that bit: 4 (the 100 in 1100).
Sibling trick of n & (n - 1): one isolates the lowest bit, the other removes it.

think.q: How many steps does while (n) n &= n - 1 take?
opts: The number of 1 bits in n
why: One step per set bit. A number with 2 set bits finishes in 2 steps, even if it is huge.
In the worst case (all bits set) it is 32 steps, so it is O(1) for 32-bit numbers anyway.

try.task: Write bitsToFlip(a, b). Return how many bits you have to flip to turn the 32-bit integer a into b (the number of positions where their bits differ). Use n & (n - 1) to count.
try.hint: a ^ b has a 1 exactly where the bits differ. Then count the 1 bits with while (x) { x &= x - 1; count++ }.

takeaway.key: n & (n - 1) removes the lowest set bit. Use it to count bits (one step per 1 bit), to test for a power of two (n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) === 0), and with XOR to count differing bits.
mistakes: Forgetting n > 0 in the power-of-two test.
Mixing up n & (n - 1) (removes the lowest bit) with n & -n (keeps only it).
Brackets: (n & (n - 1)) === 0.
Using it on numbers beyond 32 bits.

dryRun.title: Boyer-Moore voting on [2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2]
rows: count was 0, so 2 becomes the candidate
count was 0, so 1 becomes the candidate
count was 0, so 2 becomes the candidate
dryRun.note: Think of each different pair as cancelling out. The element that appears more than half of the time cannot be cancelled completely, so it is the candidate left at the end. One pass, two variables.

think.q:
let cand = null, count = 0
for (const x of [2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2]) {
  if (count === 0) cand = x
  count += x === cand ? 1 : -1
}
console.log(cand)
why: The number 2 appears four times out of seven, which is more than half. It survives the cancelling and ends as the candidate.
The trace in the table above shows how the candidate switches to 1 and back.

think.q:
let cand = null, count = 0
for (const x of [1, 2, 3]) {
  if (count === 0) cand = x
  count += x === cand ? 1 : -1
}
console.log(cand)
why: No number appears more than half the time, yet the loop still ends with a candidate: 3. The algorithm only gives the right answer if a majority exists.
When it is not guaranteed, run a second pass to count the candidate and check it.

think.q: Why can the majority element (more than n / 2 times) never be fully cancelled?
opts: Each cancel removes one majority and one other element, but there are more majority elements than all the others together
Because the count never goes below 0
why: Cancel different pairs. The others can cancel at most as many majority copies as there are others, and the majority has more copies than that.
So at least one copy of it survives.

think.q: Compared with counting in a hash map, what is the benefit of Boyer-Moore?
opts: The same O(n) time but O(1) space instead of O(n)
why: Both read the array once. The hash map stores up to n counts; Boyer-Moore stores two numbers.
Interviewers often ask for the constant-space version as a follow-up.

think.q: You want every element that appears more than n / 3 times. How many candidates can there be, and how many do you keep?
opts: At most two, so keep two candidates and two counts
why: Two different elements can each appear more than a third of the time, but three cannot (they would need more than all n slots).
Cancel in groups of three different elements, and verify both candidates at the end.

try.task: Write majorityElement(nums). Return the value that appears more than half the time, or null if there is none. Use O(1) extra space (two passes are fine).
try.hint: Pass 1: keep cand and count (Boyer-Moore). Pass 2: count how many times cand appears, and return it only if that is more than nums.length / 2.

checks.verify: assert(majorityElement([1, 1, 2, 2]) === null, "expected null, half is not more than half")

checks.t: one item and an empty array

checks.verify: const a = Array.from({ length: 200001 }, (_, i) => (i % 2 === 0 ? 7 : i)); const t0 = Date.now(); assert(majorityElement(a) === 7 && Date.now() - t0 < 100, "wrong or too slow")

takeaway.key: Boyer-Moore voting: keep a candidate and a count; equal adds, different subtracts, zero picks a new candidate. If a majority exists it survives. Verify with a second pass if it is not guaranteed. O(n) time, O(1) space.
mistakes: Trusting the candidate without checking when no majority is guaranteed.
Using "at least half" instead of "more than half".
Forgetting to reset the candidate when the count hits 0.
Using it for the n/3 version with only one candidate.

dryRun.title: KMP failure table (lps) for the pattern "abab". lps[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also its suffix
dryRun.note: When a mismatch happens at position j of the pattern, lps[j - 1] says how much of the pattern we have already matched again, so we jump back that far and never move backwards in the text. Total O(n + m).

think.q:
function lps(p) {
  const l = [0]
  let k = 0
  for (let i = 1; i < p.length; i++) {
    while (k && p[i] !== p[k]) k = l[k - 1]
    if (p[i] === p[k]) k++
    l.push(k)
  }
  return l
}
console.log(lps("aabaaab").join(","))
why: At the last letter, "aaab" ends with the same letters as the prefix "aab" for 3 characters ("aab" and "aab"), so the value is 3.
The inner while falls back along earlier table entries, like the real search does.

think.q:
function find(t, p) {
  const l = [0]
  let k = 0
  for (let i = 1; i < p.length; i++) {
    while (k && p[i] !== p[k]) k = l[k - 1]
    if (p[i] === p[k]) k++
    l.push(k)
  }
  const out = []
  k = 0
  for (let i = 0; i < t.length; i++) {
    while (k && t[i] !== p[k]) k = l[k - 1]
    if (t[i] === p[k]) k++
    if (k === p.length) { out.push(i - k + 1); k = l[k - 1] }
  }
  return out
}
console.log(find("ababa", "aba").join(","))
why: "aba" appears at index 0 and again at index 2, and the two matches share the middle "a". After a full match we set k = l[k - 1] so overlapping matches are found.
Resetting k to 0 would miss the second one.

think.q: Text length n, pattern length m. What do the naive search and KMP cost?
opts: Naive O(n * m), KMP O(n + m)
Naive O(n²), KMP O(n log n)
why: The naive way restarts from the next text position after every mismatch. KMP uses the table to keep the matched part and never moves backwards in the text.
Worst case for naive: text "aaaa...ab" and pattern "aaab".

think.q: Rabin-Karp compares hash values of windows instead of letters. What makes it fast, and what must you do on a hash match?
opts: It sorts the windows; nothing more
A rolling hash updates in O(1) when the window slides (drop the old letter, add the new one); on a match, compare the real letters because hashes can collide
It needs the table from KMP
why: The hash of the next window comes from the previous one with a couple of arithmetic steps. Equal hashes only suggest equal strings.
Rabin-Karp shines when searching for many patterns at once.

think.q: What is a sensible plan when asked "find a pattern in a text"?
opts: Start with the built-in indexOf or the naive loop, explain its worst case, and then describe (or write) KMP if asked for better
why: Most real questions are about the idea, so state the cost of the simple solution and know how the table avoids the repeated work.
Many string questions (repeated substring pattern, shortest palindrome) quietly use the same table.

try.task: Write findAll(text, pattern). Return a list of every index in text where pattern starts (matches may overlap), in increasing order. An empty pattern returns []. It must handle a text of 200,000 letters.
try.hint: Build the lps table for the pattern. Then scan the text with a pointer k into the pattern; on a full match record i - m + 1 and set k = lps[k - 1].

checks.t: the pattern equals the text, and an empty pattern
a worst case for the naive loop
checks.verify: const text = "a".repeat(200000) + "b"; const pat = "a".repeat(1000) + "b"; const t0 = Date.now(); const r = findAll(text, pat); assert(JSON.stringify(r) === "[199000]" && Date.now() - t0 < 1000, "wrong or too slow")

takeaway.key: KMP builds an lps table (longest prefix that is also a suffix) so that after a mismatch the pattern pointer falls back without moving backwards in the text: O(n + m). Rabin-Karp uses a rolling hash and must verify matches.
mistakes: Resetting the pattern pointer to 0 after a mismatch (naive O(n × m)).
Resetting to 0 after a full match and missing overlaps.
Off-by-one in the start index (i - m + 1).
Trusting a hash match without comparing the letters.

dryRun.title: Bucket sort [29, 25, 3, 49, 9, 37, 21, 43] into 5 buckets, bucket = floor(x / 10)
dryRun.note: Spread the items over buckets by value, sort each small bucket, then read the buckets in order: 3, 9, 21, 25, 29, 37, 43, 49. It is fast when the values are spread evenly over a known range.

think.q:
const nums = [29, 25, 3, 49, 9, 37, 21, 43]
const buckets = Array.from({ length: 5 }, () => [])
for (const x of nums) buckets[Math.floor(x / 10)].push(x)
const out = buckets.flatMap((b) => b.sort((p, q) => p - q))
console.log(out.join(","))
why: Items go into bucket floor(x / 10), each bucket is sorted, and flatMap joins them in bucket order.
The buckets already separate small from large, so no later step has to compare across buckets.

think.q:
const nums = [3, 1, 2, 3, 1]
const count = new Array(4).fill(0)
for (const x of nums) count[x]++
const out = []
count.forEach((c, v) => { for (let i = 0; i < c; i++) out.push(v) })
console.log(out.join(","))
why: When the values are small integers, a bucket per value is just a counter. This is counting sort: O(n + k) for values in 0..k.
It never compares two items with each other.
think.exec:
const nums = [3, 1, 2, 3, 1]
const count = new Array(4).fill(0)
for (const x of nums) count[x]++
const out = []
count.forEach((c, v) => { for (let i = 0; i < c; i++) out.push(v) })
console.log(out.join(","))

think.q: What is the time of bucket sort on n evenly spread items with about n buckets?
why: Each bucket holds only a few items, so sorting them is cheap and the total work is linear.
If everything lands in one bucket, you are sorting n items with a normal sort (O(n log n) or worse).

think.q: When is bucket sort a good choice?
opts: The values are spread fairly evenly over a known range
The values are strings of unknown length
why: You need to know the range to choose the bucket for each value, and an even spread to keep the buckets small.
For skewed data, a comparison sort (merge or quick sort) is safer.

think.q: "Top k frequent elements": count each value, then group the values by their frequency. How are the buckets arranged?
opts: Bucket index = the value; the bucket holds its count
Bucket index = the frequency (1 to n); the bucket holds the values with that frequency
Bucket index = the position in the array
One bucket for all the values
why: A frequency can never be more than n, so there are at most n buckets. Reading them from the highest index down gives the most frequent values first, in O(n).
This beats a heap (O(n log k)) when k is large.

try.task: Write topKFrequent(nums, k). Return the k values that appear most often (in any order). The tests never have a tie at the border, so the answer is unique. Aim for O(n) using buckets indexed by frequency.
try.hint: Count with a Map. Make buckets = Array.from({ length: n + 1 }, () => []) and put each value in buckets[count]. Then walk from the highest index down, collecting values until you have k.

checks.verify: const a = []; for (let i = 0; i < 100000; i++) a.push(i % 1000 === 0 ? 0 : i % 1000 < 500 ? 1 : (i % 1000) + 5000); for (let i = 0; i < 50000; i++) a.push(77777); const t0 = Date.now(); const r = topKFrequent(a, 1); assert(r.length === 1 && r[0] === 77777 && Date.now() - t0 < 500, "wrong or too slow")

takeaway.key: Bucket sort spreads items over buckets by value, sorts each small bucket and reads them in order: O(n) on average for evenly spread data. Counting sort is the one-value-per-bucket case. Buckets indexed by frequency solve "top k frequent" in O(n).
mistakes: Using it on data with an unknown or heavily skewed range.
Making buckets too few (they get crowded) or too many (wasted memory).
Forgetting to sort inside each bucket.
Using a bucket array that is too short for the biggest frequency (needs n + 1 slots).

dryRun.title: Largest rectangle in the histogram [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3]. The stack keeps bars with increasing height; a shorter bar pops taller ones
dryRun.note: When a bar is popped, the bar that arrives is its right limit (the first shorter bar) and the bar below it on the stack is its left limit. So width = i - leftIndex - 1, or the whole i if the stack is empty.

think.q:
function largest(h) {
  const st = []
  let best = 0
  const bars = [...h, 0]
  for (let i = 0; i < bars.length; i++) {
    while (st.length && bars[st[st.length - 1]] > bars[i]) {
      const height = bars[st.pop()]
      const left = st.length ? st[st.length - 1] : -1
      best = Math.max(best, height * (i - left - 1))
    }
    st.push(i)
  }
  return best
}
console.log(largest([2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3]))
why: The bars 5 and 6 side by side give a rectangle of height 5 and width 2, which is 10. No other rectangle is bigger.
The extra 0 at the end is a sentinel: it is shorter than everything, so it pops every remaining bar.

think.q: A bar is popped when bar i arrives. After the pop, the stack top (if any) is at index left. What is the width of the rectangle that uses the popped bar as its height?
why: The rectangle covers all bars strictly between the left limit (a shorter bar at left) and the right limit (the shorter bar at i). That is i - left - 1 bars.
If the stack is empty, nothing shorter is to the left, so use left = -1, which gives width i.

think.q: Why do we add a bar of height 0 at the end?
opts: It is shorter than every bar, so it forces all the bars still on the stack to be popped and measured
why: Bars that never meet a shorter bar to their right would otherwise stay on the stack unmeasured.
The same trick appears in many stack problems.

think.q: Why is the whole histogram solution O(n) even with a while inside a for?
opts: The while loop runs at most once
Every bar is pushed once and popped at most once, so the total pops are at most n
why: It is the same argument as for the next-greater element. A pop is paid for by an earlier push.
A brute force that expands from every bar would be O(n²).

think.q: Which problems are close relatives of this one, using a stack of heights?
opts: Trapping rain water, maximal rectangle in a binary matrix, and next smaller element
why: "Maximal rectangle" builds a histogram from each row of the matrix and runs this same function. Trapping rain water has a stack version too.
The question to ask is: for each item, where is the nearest smaller (or bigger) item on each side?

try.task: Write largestRectangle(heights). heights[i] is the height of a bar of width 1 in a histogram. Return the area of the biggest rectangle that fits inside the histogram. An empty list gives 0. It must run in O(n).
try.hint: Append a 0 to the heights. Keep a stack of indexes with increasing heights. When the new bar is shorter than the top, pop it, find the left limit (the new top, or -1), and compute height * (i - left - 1).

checks.t: equal bars make one wide rectangle

checks.verify: const h = Array.from({ length: 100000 }, (_, i) => i + 1); const t0 = Date.now(); assert(largestRectangle(h) === 2500050000 && Date.now() - t0 < 300, "wrong or too slow")

takeaway.key: A stack of increasing bar heights finds, for every bar, the nearest shorter bar on each side in one pass. Width = i - left - 1. Add a 0 at the end to flush the stack. O(n).
mistakes: Computing the width as i - left (off by one).
Forgetting the sentinel and leaving bars unmeasured.
Using the wrong comparison for equal heights (both work, but be consistent).
Checking every pair of bars (O(n²)).

flags: string-matching: the 200,000 letter check expects [199000]; the pattern is 1,000 a-letters followed by b at the very end of the text.
bucket-sort: topKFrequent tests avoid ties at the border by design.
monotonic-stack-2: the 100,000 rising bars answer 2,500,050,000 is the maximum of k × (n - k + 1) computed by a loop.
The dry-run tables are traced by hand (concept dry runs are not machine-run).
